# 歷體畧

## Authors / Editors

**Editions:** WYG

## Summary (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君)

Wáng Yīngmíng's 3-juan introduction to the cosmological-astronomical foundations underlying calendrical computation, completed Wànlì *rénzǐ* (1612) and printed posthumously by his son Wáng Yǎng 王懩 in Shùnzhì *bǐngxū* (1646) with diagrams supplied by Wēng Hànlín 翁漢麐. The work consists of:

**Upper *juàn* (6 chapters)**: *Tiāntǐ dìxíng* 天體地形 (heaven-body and earth-form), *Èryào* 二曜 (the two luminaries — sun and moon), *Wǔwěi* 五緯 (the five planets), *Chéncì* 辰次 (the lunar-stations and zodiacal sequence), *Kèlòu jídù* 刻漏極度 (clepsydra-divisions and polar elevation), *Záshuō* 雜説 (miscellany).

**Middle *juàn* (3 chapters)**: *Jígōng* 極宫 (the polar palaces — the asterisms around the celestial pole), *Xiàngwèi* 象位 (the asterism positions), *Tiānhàn* 天漢 (the Heavenly River — the Milky Way).

**Lower *juàn* (8 chapters)**: a separate section subtitled "*successively derived from the European books, summarizing their essentials*" (*xù jiàn Ōuluóbā shū, cuō qí tǐyào* 續見歐羅巴書，撮其體要): *Tiāntǐ dìdù* 天體地度 (heavenly-body and earthly-degrees), *Dùlǐ zhī chā* 度理之差 (degree-and-principle differences), *Wěiyào* 緯曜 (the planets), *Jīngxiù* 經宿 (the longitude-stations), *Huángdào gōngjiè* 黄道宫界 (ecliptic palace-boundaries), *Chìdào wěichán* 赤道緯纒 (equatorial latitude-and-position), *Qìhòu kèlòu* 氣候刻漏 (seasonal-nodes and clepsydra), and an appended *Lùn rìyuè jiāoshí* 論日月交食 (discussion of solar-and-lunar eclipses).

The work is unusual in the late-Wànlì astronomical literature for two reasons. First, it is among the earliest Chinese-authored works (not Jesuit-collaborated) that demonstrably integrate the European nine-spheres cosmology and the European geometric account of eclipses, despite Wáng Yīngmíng's not being a Catholic convert and not being a direct member of the Beijing residence circle — documenting the indirect spread of Ricci-period European astronomy into the broader Wànlì literati culture by 1612, two decades before the *Chóngzhēn lìshū* would formalize the synthesis. Second, the work's deliberate absence of diagrams in its original form reflects Wáng Yīngmíng's principled cosmological position — that two-dimensional representation of the spherical heavens is necessarily misleading on four specific geometric grounds (set out in Wēng Hànlín's 1646 preface).

**Abstract**

Composition: 1612 (Wànlì *rénzǐ* — the date both the 提要 and Wáng Yīngmíng's own preface affirm). Recension preserved: 1646 (Shùnzhì *bǐngxū* — Wáng Yǎng's reprint with Wēng Hànlín's diagrams), reorganized in some details from Wáng Yīngmíng's original. The *Sìkù*-preserved text reflects this 1646 recension.

The work's significance:

(a) **Indirect Jesuit influence by 1612**: the 提要's careful observation that Wáng Yīngmíng "*tacitly used*" Ricci's transmitted teachings provides precious documentation of the diffusion of Jesuit astronomical doctrine into the broader Wànlì literati community within a decade-and-a-half of Ricci's settlement in Beijing (1601). Wáng Yīngmíng was not a Catholic convert and was not a member of the inner Beijing residence circle; his absorption of the European nine-spheres cosmology and the geometric account of eclipses by 1612 demonstrates that the technical content of the new astronomy — separated from its Christian theological apparatus — was already in indirect circulation among non-Catholic Chinese astronomical specialists by the late Wànlì period.

(b) **The deliberate refusal of diagrams**: Wáng Yīngmíng's principled position that two-dimensional planar diagrams of three-dimensional celestial geometry are necessarily misleading is one of the most sophisticated late-Wànlì meditations on the limits of geometric representation. Wēng Hànlín's preface preserves the four specific geometric objections — placement of the north pole, layout of the lower hemisphere, oblique-vs-straight degree-divisions, and false outward-spreading at the southern edge — and acknowledges that any 2D diagram is merely *Gàitiān* and not *Húntiān*. This is, in effect, an early-modern Chinese articulation of what would later be called the cartographic projection problem: any planar projection of a sphere necessarily distorts.

(c) **Authorial humility and pedagogical purpose**: Wáng Yīngmíng's own preface is characteristically modest — he describes the work as composed for his son's classical study, "*kept secret in the curtain-tent, not daring to show it to others*". The decision to print only came posthumously through his son. This locates the work in the late-Wànlì tradition of family-pedagogical scholarship — not unrelated to but distinct from the more formal scholar-bureaucrat publications.

The 提要's comparison of Wáng Yīngmíng to the early-Qīng mathematicians Méi Wéndǐng and Xuē Fèngzuò 薛鳳祚 — "*[Wáng's exposition] does not match the comprehensiveness of measurement-and-computation methods later developed by [these]*" — frames the work as preparatory rather than mature: a doorway (*ménjìng* 門徑) for beginners but not the complete mathematical system. This is the standard late-imperial Chinese assessment of the late-Wànlì transitional astronomical literature.

For the broader Wànlì astronomical context, see [KR3f0008](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0008) *Gǔjīn lǜlì kǎo* (the contemporary calendar-reform agitation), [KR3f0009](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0009) *Qiánkūn tǐyì* (Ricci's foundational cosmographic primer), and [KR3f0013](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0013) *Xīnfǎ suànshū* (the eventual systematic synthesis). For Wáng Yīngmíng's biography, see [王英明](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%8B%E8%8B%B1%E6%98%8E).
